TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
FRIDAY, 17 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 4, DAY 5
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
ZELIE HEGER SC WITH DAVID ROWE,
COUNSEL ASSISTING
GABI CRAFTI SC, AUSTRALASIAN UNION OF JEWISH STUDENTS
DAVID KNOLL AM, AUSTRALIAN ACADEMIC ALLIANCE AGAINST
ANTISEMITISM
BRIN ANNIWELL, UNIVERSITY OF SYDNEY
YASSER BAKRI WITH LAILA HAMZI, AUSTRALIAN PALESTINE ADVOCACY
NETWORK
ANDREW YUILE WITH DAVID BLUMENTHAL, COMMONWEALTH OF
AUSTRALIA
JIM HARTLEY, JEWISH COUNCIL OF AUSTRALIA
DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, GROUP OF EIGHT LIMITED

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Heger.
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, I call Professor Slucki who is already in the
witness box.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<DAVID SLUCKI, AFFIRMED
MS HEGER SC: Could you please state your name?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: David Slucki.
MS HEGER SC: And you have prepared two statements for the Royal Commission.
The first is dated 3 July 2026; correct?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you have a copy of that statement there with you?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: That is still true and correct to the best of your knowledge and
belief?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, I tender that statement, which is
STAT.8999.0040.0003.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, that statement will be received in evidence.
MS HEGER SC: And you have prepared another statement dated 10 July 2026?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you have a copy of that there with you as well?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: I do.
MS HEGER SC: Is that still true and correct to the best of your knowledge and
belief?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.

MS HEGER SC: I tender that statement, which is STAT.8999.0001.0474_R.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the second statement will also be received as an exhibit.
MS HEGER SC: You are the director of the Australian Centre for Jewish
Civilisation at Monash University?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you're an historian by training?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, that's correct.
MS HEGER SC: You have written and taught about Jewish history, the Holocaust
and antisemitism since about 2007?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you received your PhD from Monash in 2010?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, that's correct.
MS HEGER SC: And as part of your role at Monash, you established the Monash
Initiative for Rapid Research into Antisemitism in 2024?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, I did.
MS HEGER SC: I will refer to that now as MIRRA, if that is convenient.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: We do love an acronym.
MS HEGER SC: Okay. And can you describe what prompted you to establish that
project at that time?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, we were watching the rise in antisemitism in
Australia. We were seeing increasing reports. We were seeing, you know, things that
the Executive Council of Australian Jewry were reporting in their annual reporting
cycle on antisemitism, and we were hearing a lot of stories. And we were, I think, as
a Jewish study centre really cognisant on our own campuses and the way we were
sort of seeing in our sector but beyond our sector.
The other thing that prompted us, I think, was we were watching a lot of public
discourse around antisemitism and we had a feeling that there wasn't good enough
yet research on the topic. And we thought it was really important that as the biggest
centre for the study of Jews and Jewish history in Australia that we should play
a major role in helping, you know, provide the evidence base so that the discussions
we have about causes, impacts, solutions would be evidence-based. Rather than, you

know, sort of instinctive or feeling what might work, we really wanted to investigate
and be able to talk, whether it's in the media, whether it was sort of informing
government or institutions, we wanted to be able to come to them and say this is the
evidence of what we're seeing and hearing and what people need, what they're asking
for, and also to sort of look around the world and see other things that are working,
that aren't working, that we can maybe start to implement in this context as well.
MS HEGER SC: And to date, MIRRA has looked at a number of different areas,
including universities; correct?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, that's correct.
MS HEGER SC: As well as the arts and creative sector?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you are in the process of looking at a number of other areas
as well?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's right. We are about to - we're just putting the
finishing touches on a report looking into Holocaust education and its role in
addressing antisemitism. By the end of this month, we will have an interim report
that looks at antisemitism in the healthcare sector. And we're also have been working
with a law firm who have helping do some legal research where antisemitism
intersects with existing federal, state and local laws.
MS HEGER SC: We will obviously focus today on the work you have done in the
sector of universities. At some point, you were tasked with developing and delivering
a training program on the antisemitism in the higher education sector. How did that
come about?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: So, in October 2024, I was asked by the Group of Eight to
join two working groups. One was focused on developing a definition of
antisemitism that would be sort of tailored to the needs of the university sector, and
the other working group was around developing a training program, both for
executive leaders and also for frontline staff, so like complaints handlers, security,
safe communities units.
And, you know, we were already working on something like that, so, you know, the
timing was actually really - really good that the Group of Eight said we need to do
this, and we were kind of waiting in the wings already developing something. So
we - that sort of put a bit of a time crunch on us when we were asked to do that. So
our aim at that point was to pilot something in the first week of December, which we
did, so within sort of less than six weeks, we really ramped it up. We put together
a research team to make sure that what we did was evidence-based, both in terms of
understanding what the problems in the sector were, or the challenges, and also in
thinking about best practice.

So we were looking at, you know, scholarship around training programs, around
educational interventions and thinking about how do those - what works the best.
What sort of seemed to work best. And so we tailored it around those things. We
also - it sort of happened in the middle of this process that there was the Senate
Inquiry into Antisemitism at Universities or the hearings to have an inquiry, and, you
know, there were something like five or six hundred testimonies that people
submitted to that inquiry.
So one of our researchers put together a database of those testimonies and did some
coding around those, also then also the ECAJ and 5A and the CSG Victoria were
really generous in sharing some of the materials they'd collected with us. And what
we wanted to be able to do was when we were developing the training, we wanted to
have a series of different kinds of case studies that we could deploy, depending on
the needs of the university. So they covered things like, you know, controversy over
posters, things in classrooms, comments in classrooms. Interpersonal conflict on
campus.
What we really wanted to do was capture the grey areas. We thought it was - there
were things that were pretty straightforward; right. Someone is marching doing
a Nazi salute, like, that is pretty clearly antisemitic. And we didn't feel we needed to
cover those what I would say are more black and white instances. We really wanted
to have the people in the room talking about where are there shades of grey, where
are there areas where academic freedom or freedom of speech intersect with
questions around inclusion and safety, and then really use the trainings to generate
productive discussions in those rooms.
So it was process - I would say it was about six weeks from being asked to do it to
launching the first pilot which was for the Monash vice-chancellors group, and they
were generous enough to be our guinea pigs. That was a two-hour session. The next
week we trialled a four-hour session with a Group of Eight working group. We
landed in the middle on three hours as a kind of happy medium where we could
cover everything without sort of overdoing it, I guess.
And then the next six months of actually rolling it out, we just were continually
tweaking it, and I would say we are still continually tweaking as we go and trying to
figure out constantly what works best.
MS HEGER SC: I see. I will ask you in a moment about some more detail about the
content of the training, but as you set out in your statement, at the moment the
training, has been delivered to about 1600 leaders and frontline staff at about 30
different universities?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: As well as to -

PROFESSOR SLUCKI: I think we're now - the last figures I saw yesterday, we are
now over 1700.
MS HEGER SC: Okay.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: So, yes, it's not - we don't measure success by bums on
seats but we are sort of really happy that we're getting that coverage as well.
MS HEGER SC: You've also delivered the training to teams at the Commonwealth
Department of Education, TEQSA, Universities Australia and the Group of Eight?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct, some of whom are in the room today.
MS HEGER SC: As well as a university in New Orleans?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, Tulane University in New Orleans, and actually
they've invited me back later this year to run another series of the trainings for more
groups of their leaders.
MS HEGER SC: I see. And up until the present point, to what extent has that rollout
been funded and staffed by Monash University itself?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: It's been a mixture in terms of funding. So Monash
supported particularly the research phase and the inquiry phase early on. So Monash
provided the funding for research assistance. When it came time to me going out and
leading the trainings for the Group of Eight, the universities themselves bore those
costs, and that was the administrative support of the Group of Eight. In June last
year, we ran a session where we trained a team of facilitators and that was
supported ASECA, by the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, and Universities
Australia. So that allowed us to really expand the footprint of the trainings. And it
also meant it didn't depend on one person and me to do that. And so, you know, it's
meant we can reach a whole lot more people across different levels of the university.
MS HEGER SC: There has now been a contribution of 1.5 million from the
Commonwealth Government to support that work?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct, over two years from the Department of
Education.
MS HEGER SC: So could I then ask you a bit about the theory underlining the
training program and some of its content. You note at paragraph 21 of your first
statement that it's tied to what you describe as the theory of change. Could you just
tell us a built more about what that theory entails.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, the thing that principally underpins what we are
doing is - you know, we see it as really important to have a kind of partnership model
with universities that we want to support them and help them and we don't want an

antagonistic relationship. I don't believe it would be that helpful for me to come in
and point fingers. So that's kind of the basis of everything, is how do we understand
the needs of university leaders, how do we understand the needs of the complaints
handling staff who picks up a phone call from a student in distress. How do we help
support them to understand what they don't - might not understand what's behind that
distress.
And, you know, so the other part of our theory of change is we don't expect to train
one and a half million students and 130,000-odd academics. What we really want to
do is be targeted in our approach. So we are trying to think of where can we have the
maximum impact. So what we're doing with this training program is focusing on
leaders and decision-makers, and whether that's a vice-chancellor who has to make
overarching policy decisions, or a head of department who receives a complaint from
a student and has to make a call on what to do with that, or a security staff member
who in the moment is trying to make a determination over something that is often
really complex in that environment.
We want to help support those decision-making processes and we think that the
downstream impact of that will really - it will help create robust campus
environments. And the final thing I should say about our theory of change is - and
I can't emphasise this strongly enough. And I should say that what I'm about to say is
not my formulation. It's actually someone said this to me last week, and I thought it
was so elegant that I'm going to steal it.
And that is that if we are only solving for antisemitism, we are not solving
antisemitism. So what really underpins our work is the idea that all the work we do
should also create frameworks, models that can be tweaked, applied, help support all
the ways in which we are trying to tackle discrimination across the sector. That is
true, I would say, of all the MIRRA work that we do. Any sector we are looking at,
we're thinking of how do we tackle antisemitism and how do we understand
antisemitism as symptomatic of bigger issues that we are facing in Australian
society?
MS HEGER SC: What sort of issues are you referring to there?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: I mean I think the principal one that we're really conscious
of is polarisation and the ways in which - one thing I've observed - and I'm certainly
not alone or a pioneer in this, but one thing I've observed over and over is this sense
that - there's a kind of all or nothing thinking that pervades public discourse and
political debate, and so it's not only that we disagree, but actually when we disagree
with someone, we see them as wrong and as bad or evil. And I think that's the kind
of thing we want to start pulling the Australian public away from, the idea that
actually we all come to these things with a great deal of sincerity.
You know, one thing I say at the beginning of every training is we've all watched the
violence and the events in the Middle East, whether in Israel or Gaza or Lebanon or
Iran or wherever, we watch with a great deal of distress. And much of the kind of

anger, hurt, trauma we see, whoever it is, comes from a place of hurt. And we want
to encourage people to see that as the starting point when we sort of enter these
conversations. And that is true for Jewish staff and students who feel traumatised by
October 7. It's true for Palestinian and Muslim staff and students who are also
traumatised by what they're witnessing on a daily basis. We don't think it should be
an either/or proposition.
MS HEGER SC: You go on to describe some of the themes in the training that is
delivered. One part, you say, deals with the basics of Judaism and addressing Jewish
diversity. Why is that important? Starting with the basic of Judaism, why is that an
important first step to help people understand.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: It's interesting, because that wasn't originally part of the
training that we ran. We actually sort of started with this - and I'm a historian so
I kind of got really excited to teach history and the history of antisemitism, weirdly,
but actually we realised pretty quickly there's actually a need for some basic literacy
in who the Jews of Australia are. And, basically, we developed this idea pretty early
on that actually what's as important to teach in what antisemitism is, is teaching who
are the Jews of Australia, because if you can't understand that, you can't really
understand, I don't think, what lies at the heart of people's trauma, their angst.
You know, to be able to understand what Judaism is, who Jews are in all our
different shapes and sizes, what are the different things that Jews believe? How does
that manifest? What's the impact, for example, of the Holocaust and the impact of
intergenerational trauma. So all these things, we thought it was really important to
lay that foundation so that people could actually understand where the distress is
coming from and why we're not just talking about, say, hurt feelings. Right? It's - or
even if we're talking about hurt feelings, like, that's something we should try and
understand and take seriously.
MS HEGER SC: When you refer to addressing the diversity of the Jewish people,
what sort of diversity are you referring to?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: In all its forms, so whether that's religious observance and
the kind of spectrum of religious observance - and this is where I get in trouble with
the training, a little bit, because I spend too much time having fun talking about
different perceptions of God and laws and the way that Jews practice these things or
don't practice them. We also talk about ethnic and cultural diversity, so we focus on
the difference between Ashkenazi Jews - Jews who trace their lineage to
Europe - and Sephardi Jews, who trace their lineage to the expulsion from Spain to
North Africa and the Middle East particularly.
We talk about Israeli society and the ways in which waves of refugees that have
come to Israel sort of mean that it's actually a really complex story in terms of, like,
the Jewish history of that place. So, you know, we're really trying to show that
people shouldn't make assumptions about - just because someone is Jewish, about
what they - how about how they're Jewish.

Another thing we bring into that is we look at data from the Gen17 survey which was
conducted by my predecessor, Andrew Markus, along with Dr David Graham from
the Jewish Communal Appeal in New South Wales. And I will add that Gen17 is
nine year old data and we are actually about to launch the next iteration of that
survey. So by the end of this year we will have more up-to-date data.
But, basically, we look at a couple of the questions that got asked there to talk about
what does being Jewish mean to Australian Jews? And there's really - you see the
"Aha" moments that people have when I say, in 2017, only 46 per cent of Australian
Jews thought believing in God was important to their Jewishness. 95 per cent said
remembering the Holocaust was important to their Jewishness.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just -
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes, sorry, I'm nerding out a little bit.
COMMISSIONER: Sorry to interrupt, but can I just, at that point, when you
reference the number of Australian Jews who thought remembering the Holocaust
was important, we keep being told that Australia has a very large proportion of the
Jewish community have a history of Holocaust survival.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And a little earlier you spoke of intergenerational trauma. Is
that relevant to understanding the level of distress for Australian Jews of October 7?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Absolutely. Yes, I mean, I think - I would say that and
more. To understand the ways in which - and, again, I would say this is probably true
across the political spectrum. So if you're talking about anti-Zionist Jews or Zionist
Jews or whatever, you know, the impact of the Holocaust animates the way people
think about what it means to be Jewish. Just to give a bit of a sense of that, in 1933
there were 22,000 Jews in Australia. And by - that's when the Nazis assumed power
in Germany. By 1961, there were over 60,000. So there's this critical mass of the
Australian Jewish community that are descended from Holocaust survivors.
And so most of us - not all of us, but most of us grew up with grandparents who lost
their whole families, who survived the worst conditions. They had then raised their
children - traumatised people raising children not always - I just - you know, I don't
want to talk for everyone, but I think about my own family and what that must have
been like, to have been raised by people who, you know, had such a rupture in their
life, and then the kind of knock-on impact that has.
So the way I always talk about it is not that I have capital-T trauma from the
Holocaust, but the way that, you know, we live our lives is really shaped by whatever
message we take from that, and that's different for different people, but it's a really
powerful sort of factor in why - you know, why people are hypersensitive about

antisemitism particularly. And why, you know, we do think it's really important to
address it, even in its smallest forms because we sort of know that nothing is in
isolation; one thing can lead to the next thing.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MS HEGER SC: You note that the training also addresses, to some extent, Zionism
and anti-Zionism, and if I could just use that as a launching pad for the article that
you annexed to your statement, which is STAT.8999.0040.0007. And that's an article
that you wrote in The Guardian entitled In the Battle of Antisemitism We Must
Accept That Zionism Means Different Things to Different People.
If I could just go to the second page of that and ask you about a couple of points.
About halfway down the page you have noted:
"Today many Jews..."
And I take you it, you emphasise many Jews and not all Jews:
"...see Zionism as a modern continuation of centuries-old yearning for connection
with the land of Israel, which is deeply rooted in Jewish history and liturgy."
And you go on to note in the next paragraph, however, that there is no consensus
even between those who are Zionist on what that self-determination ought to look
like. Could you just speak to the range of views on that topic?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes. I mean, there's been throughout the sort
of - throughout the history of Judaism there have been many different views on what
this sense of return means. So it is in the liturgy. You know, still today - you know,
when I prayed this morning, you know, we talk about redemption and the
resurrection of the temple in Jerusalem, and that has been a consistent theme for
really thousands of years. And there has been a variety of ways in which people have
written and thought about that in those intervening thousands of years.
The term Zionism as a concept emerges in the 1880s, 1890s as a response
particularly to antisemitism, to rising antisemitism in Europe, and also to the sort of
political wings of Europe too. And, you know, it meant something particular in that
moment and that was the idea that one response to antisemitism was that there ought
to be Jewish national sovereignty, they settled on in the historic Jewish homeland in
Palestine. There were other movements that said there should be a Jewish state in
other parts of the world. They were more marginal, I would say.
But that changes over time as well, you know, as the world changes, as politics
changes. You know, obviously a big change is the establishment of the State of
Israel. So what does Zionism mean in that context when you have established it? So
at various - for many people at that time, Zionism is around the in-gathering of the

Jewish population into the new State of Israel. For others, it's about Israel as sort of
cultural spiritual centre. And, again, it continues to evolve as the world evolves.
So today I would say that, you know, most people - perhaps all people, I guess, who
identify as Zionist would say what that means to them is the basic idea that there
ought to be a Jewish state somewhere in the historic land of Israel, the land of Israel
as distinct from the state. The land of Israel is what the Bible describes. And then
beyond that, there's a spectrum of views. So you know when people kind of use
"Zionist" as an epithet, it's not actually capturing what the person who is using it to
describe themselves means.
And so one of the reasons I wrote this piece - I mean I was asked to write it by the
editors at The Guardian, but - and it was right after the Bondi massacre, and there
was just the discourse around Zionism and what constitutes antisemitism or not was
just bubbling over. So I thought it was really important to, like, help paint that
picture to distinguish that these terms are not so simplistic.
MS HEGER SC: You have noted here that for those who are Zionist and believe in
that concept of self-determination in a land of Israel, even for those, some, of course,
say there should be a democratic Jewish state alongside a democratic Palestinian
state.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And for those Zionists, many of them are still deeply critical or
even, as you say, hostile to the current Israeli government?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: That view is entirely compatible with being a Zionist.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes. Absolutely.
MS HEGER SC: You go on to observe that:
"For Palestinians and critics of Zionism..."
for some of them:
"...the term signals displacement, inequality and the ongoing suffering of
Palestinians since the establishment of the Israeli state."
Can you just speak to that point?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes. And this is where I think we are often in this
discussion talking at cross-purposes where, you know, people in Jewish community
are saying, "To me, Zionism is about my attachment to this place" and, you know,

there's religious, cultural, historic reasons for that attachment and there's also a lot of
people feel that there are, like, existential reasons for it. And many will point to the
Holocaust as an example of what animates their attachment to the State of Israel.
And on the flip side, it's very true that, you know, for Palestinians, the establishment
of the Jewish state also had consequences. And, you know, one of the things when
we teach about, you know, the Arab-Israeli conflict in university classrooms, like,
one of the things we talk about a lot is the conflicting and contested narratives that,
you know, for both peoples there is tremendous pain that accompanies the history of
this place.
And, you know, sometimes those narratives are in conflict and it's hard to square
them. But I think what I'm trying to get at in this piece and in all our work is to sort
of show people, like, actually the person sitting opposite you is coming at this with
a lot of pain and fear, and we need to recognise that as a starting point.
COMMISSIONER: Looking at Australian Jews, Professor, the Macquarie
dictionary helpfully defines Zionism post-1948 simply in terms of "support for
Israel". An Australian Zionist of my age, that would translate into support for Israel
under the government of Yitzhak Rabin and support for Israel under the present
administration, widely different as the two administrations are, because what
"support" means is support for the idea of the homeland in Israel for Jewish people.
I mean, is that a fair way of describing it?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: I think so. I would add, though, that many people are
conflicted as well because they're attached to the State of Israel but they have
a vision for what that state ought to look like. And so, I mean, I don't think - most
people don't want violence. You know, they don't want to see endless conflict. They
want to see peace in the region. And I think the sort of - and we'll investigate this
a little further so we can get some, like, pretty clear data from it in the upcoming
Gen26 survey, but my sense is most Australian Jews want to see a two-state solution
in Israel. So they do support the idea that there ought to be a Jewish state alongside
a Palestinian state.
And then there is this question of what does that Jewish state look like? And there's
so much conflict in Israel about what that looks like, about the religious nature of the
state or how secular it ought to be, or things around compulsory military service or
things around gender equality or rights for LGBTQIA people. You know, in a world
in which there's, like, this tension between the secular and religious Jewish Israeli
world.
And so, you know, there's this attachment and this support for Israel to, you know, be
a robust democratic state. But I do think there's been a lot of concern in recent years
around whether or not, you know, it upholds its sort of promise for liberalism or
illiberalism or - yes, I mean, people - there's not consensus within the Jewish
community on these questions. I think that's the important thing. Like, even among

people who identify as Zionist, there's still a wide range of views of what it means to
be attached to that place.
COMMISSIONER: But if you have that attachment, it's very difficult to, as it were,
denounce Israel because you don't approve of the actions of the present
administration.
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: Yes. I think what you are pointing to is a really interesting
phenomenon that we have seen emerge in the discourse, and that is a distinction
between criticising Israel - so someone who is, you know, maybe they've been
opposed to Israel's actions or whatever, or to the government's actions, but they're
very much attached to the idea of there being a strong Jewish state, and on the other
hand, the idea that Israel ought not exist.
And increasingly I think it's become really hard in parts - I think about our sector -it's
become increasingly hard to say, yes, I criticise Israel and I think Israel should exist,
because there are parts of this discourse where you say, well, as long as Israel
exists - you know, I think we've heard at various points throughout these hearings as
well, you know, Israel simply existing is a problem in some parts of this political
discussion. So I think that's really hard for many Jews to hold, is being able to say we
want to see Israel be a particular kind of thing but we want it to be a thing.
MS HEGER SC: That's - it's a complicated issue. How do you go about addressing
that in a three-hour training session?
PROFESSOR SLUCKI: That's a really good question. So, I mean, everything we
do is scholarly, and that's really the basis of the trainings. Particularly approaching
the university sector, we thought it was really important that - you know, I approach
it basically like I would approach a classroom, to say here's the range of different
ways of looking at this position. So when we talk about Zionism and anti-Zionism,
what we don't say is "Zionism is this" and "anti-Zionism is this". What we say is
actually these things are spectrums and they mean different things across those
spectrums.
So one of the things we talk about is whether it's politics, whether it's a matter of
identity, whether it's a matter of simply Judaism. So, for many people, they say, well,
Zionism is Judaism, to me. And then other people - this is where I feel very sorry for
vice-chancellors, who, they have someone - like, leaders in the Jewish community
say Zionism is Judaism, and then they have other people from other parts of the
world say Zionism isn't Judaism, and they're sort of looking at that thinking, "How
do I navigate this tension?"
So what we're trying to do is not answer that question for them, but actually to
present them with the spectrum of what these things mean so that they can make
informed and meaningful decisions and actually understand what the people that are
coming to them are telling them. I think maybe that's something that's gone missing

in the sector is, you know, just we need better literacy around these things. Not just

across providers, particularly for responding to those issues around external actors.
So it was intended to particularly both share good practice with the sector, and keep
focus on the fact that we expected them to take very active responses.

consultation, we would, at a minimum, expect to direct providers to both the IHRA

should consider.
MS HEGER SC: And when this standard was being developed - sorry, I withdraw

2025?
DR RUSSELL: It was.

DR RUSSELL: For a number of reasons. The structure of the standards is
intentionally at a level of principles, and that is, in part, to ensure that they have
stability and applicability over time, but also to recognise that individual providers
with different circumstances may need to make different choices about how they go
about meeting the standards.
It was also our view and the advice that we had that because providers have separate
obligations at law arising from relevant Commonwealth and state and territory
legislation, that providers needed to ensure that a definition that they adopted
enabled them to meet those respective obligations. But I would say particularly that
because the nature of providers' activity varies, they also need to make sure that
a definition can be applied for the type of issues that arise.

research or academic or scholarly activity around political science might be very
different from the questions that might arise in a provider that is focused entirely on

MS HEGER SC: So while at that stage you had a large number of universities

scholarship, as well as being applied in the negative when there are concerns that
obligations may not have been met.
MS HEGER SC: And by incorporating into policies that regulate staff and student
conduct, your expectation is not that the definition would just be noted or footnoted,
but that would be incorporated into the substantive obligation on staff and students
not to engage in racism or other forms of profitability conduct?
DR RUSSELL: Noting that this is very new, my expectation is that it
would - providers would ensure that they confer obligations and expectations not to
engage in racism.
MS HEGER SC: Including antisemitism as they have defined it?
DR RUSSELL: Including antisemitism as they have defined it.

processes, and in two senses. In one sense that there needs to be annual reporting of
de-identified data, but then we also had some instances where a staff member or
student said "Actually, there should have been a public statement on the outcome of
this particular complaint in order to give the university community some confidence
that consequences resulted for this particular situation." What's your view on both of
those types of reporting?
DR FINKEL AC: So on the first one which is reporting de-identified consolidated
data, I think there's no conflict there. There's, if I can use the vernacular, it's
a no-brainer. Universities should be doing it. The police want to see those kinds of
reports. The community wants to see those reports. And councils, everybody can
learn from those reports, especially over a number of years when you are looking
longitudinally at the changes to the statistics.
Going public on individual cases is really complicated because both parties, the
complainant and the person being complained about, have privacy rights, and so that
has to be dealt with very, very carefully. And it's part of the reason, not the only
reason, why those sorts of issues should be escalated to a very high level where
a deputy vice-chancellor can - it's not even easy to make the call because sometimes
they've got legally protected rights. But the deputy vice-chancellor can at least
engage with people to try to determine whether it would be to everybody's benefit to
have a public discussion. But that might not be that often because one party or the
other will have legally enforceable privacy rights. We can't override that.
MS HEGER SC: You mentioned the importance of training at least complaints staff
to deal with complaints and, of course, the topic of training is something you've dealt
with more broadly in your report. In terms of training for both staff and students,
obviously it would be ideal if everybody could receive training on antisemitism as

well as Islamophobia as well other forms of racism. How do you balance the need for
that against the size and scale of universities populations?
DR FINKEL AC: Yes, it's a difficult challenge. I think we've come up with a pretty
reasonable approach doing it by dividing the student and staff population into five
cohorts. So we divided the student population into all of the incoming students, and
a subset of those being student leaders. It's not practical - no one felt that it was
practical to have in-person training on racism, antisemitism and other issues related
to good decent social behaviour for every single student. Numbers are just too big
every single year.
So, for those, we recommended that there be online racism training modules
consistent with what was done on academic integrity and gender-based violence and
things like that. And that can be done effectively, and we've got an example in there,
I think it's the University of Queensland work in that area as an example, that every
university would do it their own way but it's good to have an example to go along
with the recommendation.
But for the two or three per cent of students who have leadership roles in the clubs or
societies or residential leaders or sports groups or the editors of student media, we
felt that they should engage in deeper training through an in-person training. And for
that, again, we were not prescriptive, universities should decide what that in-person
training should be. But it should be substantial. And we put in there as an example
the Brave Conversations program that was developed over the last few years at
Monash University, because it came to us again and again through our consultations,
as an example of an excellent training program on Constructive Disagreement, it's
called Brave Conversations but it's talking about how do you engage difficult topics
without ad hominem attacks and actually being in deep disagreement, but at least
engage with each other and advance the discussion.
And that's a program that is typically the better part of a day, for 100 people in
a room, and it's been very, very well received by participants who have been through
it. As leaders, they can then propagate what they learn - to some extent
anyway - through to their student colleagues. So that's two of the five cohorts. Shall
I keep going?
MS HEGER SC: Yes, please do.
DR FINKEL AC: Okay. So for the staff, we identified three cohorts: the executive
leadership, the professional staff and then tutors and lecturers, the ones who are
engaging in education. We felt that the Brave Conversations program, as an example,
is the type of in-person training that tutors and lecturers should go through, because
you want to have discussions in class that are amiable, even if there's deep
disagreement because students have different perspectives, lecturers have different
perspectives. No one should be shut down. Opinions should be allowed, and lecturers
and tutors should be well trained on how to manage that classroom decorum, if you
like.

That leaves the professional staff and the executive leadership. And for both of those,
we recommended that they have training on understanding the nature of antisemitism
in contemporary Australia, how to recognise it and what are the leadership and
consultative responses that they need to be able to deliver to deal with issues as they
arrive. And, again, we were not prescriptive about what courses they do, but we did
say it should be an in-person course, and the example that came to us again and
again, which we then put in as an example, was the leadership training program that I
think David Slucki - Professor Slucki was advising you on this morning, the ACJC
Leadership Training Program.
So those were the five cohorts that we defined. I think it's manageable. It sounds
enormous task to provide in-person training for thousands of staff at a university, but
they do do professional development training from time to time. There are
expectations on them. And if you do the numbers, they could get through, if they
wanted to, most or all of their staff in a year if they implement a program in
a sensible fashion.
MS HEGER SC: I see. Has the reaction to that proposal from universities been
positive so far, in your experience?
DR FINKEL AC: It has. It has. I had the pleasure of delivering a report on 4 June to
the Group of Eight board, the vice-chancellors, and they were verbally pretty
comfortable with all of the recommendations that we made.
MS HEGER SC: Thank you, Dr Finkel. I have no further questions.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Perhaps I've just got a couple, Professor. Just turning to
the French Model Code, I think the background to that were a series of instances in
which students were suppressing freedom of speech by deplatforming people with
whose views they didn't agree, and it was against that background that Robert French
was asked to look at the issue of freedom of speech at universities. And I think he
then mounted a really quite comprehensive inquiry distinguishing freedom of speech,
on the one hand, from academic freedom on the other. And concluding that whilst
there was not a crisis in freedom of speech, universities had different policies and
procedures, and so he devised a Model Code recommending that it be adopted by
universities and that it have priority when there was any inconsistency with
a university's other practices; is that a fair account?
DR FINKEL AC: I believe so.
COMMISSIONER: And then I think Professor Sally Walker was commissioned by
government to assess the extent to which the universities were aligning themselves
with the Model Code as Mr French had recommended. Again, is that your
understanding?
DR FINKEL AC: That is my understanding.

COMMISSIONER: All right. All I'm seeking to get to is whether - your committee,
I think, proposed in recommendation 4 that there should be work done with the
Federal Government to review the French Model Code to ensure that it remains
optimal in responding to contemporary manifestations of antisemitism while
continuing to uphold freedom of speech and academic freedom.
DR FINKEL AC: Correct.
COMMISSIONER: And, in particular, you recommended a change, and that related
to the duty to support the wellbeing of students and staff. That is the only change that
your committee recommended. Is it proposed that there be some further review, or
otherwise was your committee happy with the French Model Code subject to that
one change?
DR FINKEL AC: I would say, Commissioner, that all of my committee has
enormous respect for the Model Code proposed by Robert French. But it was brought
to us again and again and again that circumstance change and things need to be
looked at again. We looked at it, and we saw one particular piece where we felt that
there needed to be a modernisation to align with, say, the Hate legislation that the
Federal Government passed where the burden was previously in the code - and I can't
remember the exact words; maybe somebody can bring it up - but basically was
talking about intent to offend or -
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
DR FINKEL AC: Or incite hatred and actual acts that incite hatred. And it was
using the word "or", which means that if you were clearly inciting hatred or violence
but claiming that that wasn't your intent, then you really wouldn't be subject to the
coverage of the French Model Code. The more modern thinking is that one or the
other is sufficient to express concern. So we gave as an example a single word
change from "and" to "or" as one of the modernisations that should be considered.
We didn't think it was appropriate for us to go through and do a full review, but
given that people were expressing to us that they felt times had changed - I mean,
you have had the onslaught of social media. You've had the shift to online learning
after COVID.
You have had the incidences in the last few years where protests on campus weren't
against university policy or government policy; they were against things that
were - and expressing hatred of fellow students. These were things that weren't the
norm in 2019 or leading up to 2019, and so we felt it was appropriate that there
should be some sort of consideration. So all that we recommended was that the
vice-chancellors seek to engage with the government to have a discussion about
reviewing the French Model Code, but we did not want to be prescriptive.
COMMISSIONER: The Go8 members, do they subscribe to the model code?

DR FINKEL AC: They do.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
DR FINKEL AC: They do. It's not an enforceable code to my understanding, but
